hook: Between 1950 and 1995, Marion Tinsley lost seven games of checkers. Total.
story: He was a mathematics professor with a doctorate in combinatorial analysis, and he was so far ahead of everyone else that he once quit the game for twelve years out of boredom. In 1990 he agreed to play a computer program called Chinook. Ten moves into the tenth game, Chinook's programmer made his move, and Tinsley looked up and said, "You're going to regret that." The programmer thought his machine was winning; by his own account it needed sixty moves of lookahead to see it had already lost.
number: By most counts that's seven losses in forty-five years, across thousands of games. The New York Times said nine; either way, nobody in any mind sport has been that good for that long.
closer: Two of the seven were to the computer.
full_text: Between 1950 and 1995, Marion Tinsley lost seven games of checkers. Total. He was a mathematics professor with a doctorate in combinatorial analysis, and he was so far ahead of everyone else that he once quit the game for twelve years out of boredom. In 1990 he agreed to play a computer program called Chinook. Ten moves into the tenth game, Chinook's programmer made his move, and Tinsley looked up and said, "You're going to regret that." The programmer thought his machine was winning; by his own account it needed sixty moves of lookahead to see it had already lost. By most counts that's seven losses in forty-five years, across thousands of games. The New York Times said nine; either way, nobody in any mind sport has been that good for that long. Two of the seven were to the computer.
